key_findings: COPE released a position statement on February 13, 2023, establishing that AI tools cannot be listed as authors of academic papers because they cannot take legal responsibility for work, cannot assert conflicts of interest, and cannot manage copyright/license agreements. The guidelines mandate transparent disclosure of AI tool usage in Methods/Acknowledgements sections. AI use is categorized as assistive (grammar/language tools, no disclosure needed) or generative (content-producing tools, disclosure required). Detection tools have significant limitations and should not be sole basis for rejections. Enforcement of voluntary disclosure remains challenging due to technical limitations in detecting AI-generated content.
methodology: Policy document analysis and position statement review. COPE consulted with member organizations (WAME, JAMA Network, Springer Nature, Elsevier) to develop consensus-based guidance on AI authorship standards.
sample_size: International policy affecting hundreds of journals and thousands of publishers; COPE has 10,000+ members and 10+ affiliated organizations
geographic_scope: Global — COPE is an international organization providing guidance adopted by major publishers worldwide (Europe, North America, Asia-Pacific regions)
publication_details: COPE Position Statement on Authorship and AI Tools, February 13, 2023. Available at: https://publicationethics.org/guidance/cope-position/authorship-and-ai-tools. Also covered in COPE Focus on Artificial Intelligence series and follow-up discussions on emerging AI dilemmas in scholarly publishing.
replication_status: COPE guidelines have been adopted and replicated by major publishers including Springer Nature, Elsevier, Sage, Wiley, and others. Comparable guidance issued by ICMJE (International Committee of Medical Journal Editors) in May/January 2023-2024, WAME (World Association of Medical Editors), confirming convergence on core principles across major editorial organizations.
methodological_limitations: The guidelines rely on voluntary disclosure rather than technical enforcement mechanisms. Detection tools for AI-generated content are imperfect and cannot distinguish between assisted vs. authored content. The framework does not address sufficiently how journals should handle undisclosed AI use or provide systematic monitoring protocols. Limited empirical data on compliance rates or effectiveness of disclosure policies in practice.
generalizability: Highly generalizable to Vietnam's higher education and research sectors. The principles are internationally applicable and align with global research integrity standards. Vietnamese universities adopting international publication standards would benefit from implementing similar AI disclosure policies. However, enforcement capacity in Vietnamese institutions may require additional institutional support and training.
which_debate_claim_it_supports_or_challe: Supports: (1) Academic integrity concerns about undisclosed AI use in student assignments — guidelines establish that transparency and responsibility are core to authorship. (2) Research integrity protection — systematic disclosure requirements can reduce fraud and hallucinated citations. Challenges: (1) Claims that AI detection is easy or reliable — COPE acknowledges detection tools are imperfect. (2) Arguments for complete AI prohibition — COPE allows assistive AI use without disclosure. (3) Assumption that disclosure mandates are easily enforceable — COPE identifies voluntary disclosure as challenge.
policy_implications: Vietnamese HE institutions should: (1) Adopt clear AI disclosure policies aligned with COPE standards, distinguishing assistive vs. generative AI. (2) Develop Faculty and student training on AI authorship ethics and disclosure requirements. (3) Include AI use disclosure as standard in submission forms and rubrics. (4) Establish reviewer guidelines for flagging suspected undisclosed AI use. (5) Review detection tool limitations before deploying anti-plagiarism systems. (6) Consider incentive structures that reduce pressure to publish high volumes, which may encourage unethical AI use.
how_it_changes_the_analysis: COPE guidelines provide an international evidence-based framework that validates the concern about academic integrity in AI-assisted writing, while also clarifying that some AI use (assistive) is acceptable if properly disclosed. The guidelines shift the debate from 'AI is bad' to 'transparency and responsibility are essential.' For the Vietnamese EdTech research, this evidence supports developing ethical AI use frameworks rather than blanket prohibitions. The identified limitations in enforcement (voluntary disclosure + weak detection) suggest that institutional culture change around research integrity may be more important than technical detection approaches.
contradictory_findings: Alternative argument: Some scholars argue that disclosure of writing assistance (human or AI) should be voluntary rather than mandated, since human editors and writing services are not always disclosed. [uncertain] COPE does not fully address this symmetry. Additionally, some journals have adopted more restrictive policies (prohibiting generative AI entirely) that go beyond COPE guidance, suggesting disagreement about optimal stringency. Counterargument: [uncertain] It is unclear how many journals have actually implemented COPE guidelines vs. how many have adopted stricter or more lenient policies.
alternative_interpretations: Interpretation 1: COPE's distinction between assistive and generative AI is pragmatic and risk-based — only content-producing AI requires disclosure because only that poses integrity risks. Interpretation 2: The distinction is arbitrary and underestimates risks from 'assistive' grammar tools that can change meaning and introduce bias. Interpretation 3: COPE's focus on disclosure rather than prevention assumes authors will honestly self-report AI use, but incentive structures (publish-or-perish pressure) may lead to non-disclosure despite policies. Interpretation 4: The framework is author-centric but may miss institutional pressures (e.g., predatory journals accepting undisclosed AI for faster publication cycles).
unresolved_questions: What is the actual compliance rate for AI disclosure among authors submitting to journals that require it?
How effective are current AI detection tools in practice, and what is the false positive/negative rate by field?
Should disclosure requirements differ for different types of AI (LLMs vs. image generation vs. statistical analysis software)?
How should institutions handle retrospective discovery of undisclosed AI use in already-published papers?
What role should institutional review boards (IRBs) play in monitoring AI use in student research and theses?
How can voluntary disclosure mandates be enforced without compromising trust in peer review?
Are there cultural or linguistic barriers to implementing COPE guidelines in non-English-speaking research communities?

Member organizations: WAME (World Association of Medical Editors), JAMA Network, Springer Nature, Elsevier, Sage Publishing, Wiley, Wolters Kluwer
funding_sources: COPE is supported by membership fees from publishers and organizations; no specific external funding source identified for this guidance. Guidance development was collaborative across major STM (scientific, technical, medical) publishers.
what_evidence_still_missing: Empirical data on: (1) Actual compliance rates with AI disclosure policies across journal submissions and fields. (2) Accuracy of AI detection tools in identifying undisclosed AI use (false positive/negative rates by field, language, model). (3) Institutional implementation rates of COPE guidelines in universities, particularly outside North America and Western Europe. (4) Effectiveness of different enforcement mechanisms (reviewer flags, editorial audits, author training). (5) Comparative impact of voluntary vs. mandatory disclosure policies. (6) Cost-benefit analysis of implementing AI disclosure vs. detection vs. prohibition policies in institutions. (7) Cultural and linguistic adaptability of COPE guidelines in non-English research communities.
recommended_studies: Large-scale survey of journal editors and publishers to document actual adoption of COPE guidelines (vs. alternative policies) 18-24 months after publication
Empirical compliance study: audit random sample of journal submissions to determine rate of undisclosed AI use vs. disclosed use
Meta-analysis of AI detection tools (GPTZero, Turnitin AI detection, Originality AI) across domains: measure accuracy, false positive/negative rates, limitations by field
Case study research: implementation of COPE guidelines in Vietnamese universities — barriers, institutional responses, faculty/student understanding
Comparative policy analysis: map journal AI policies worldwide; identify deviation from COPE vs. ICMJE guidance; analyze reasons for divergence
Longitudinal study: track effect of AI disclosure policies on publication ethics misconduct reports (3-5 years post-implementation)
Qualitative research: author interviews about motivations for/against disclosing AI use; how incentive structures affect disclosure behavior
feasibility_of_filling_gap: High feasibility (18-24 months, moderate cost): Survey studies and policy mapping are low-cost and feasible. Compliance audits require journal cooperation but are feasible. Case studies in Vietnamese universities are feasible within institutional contexts. Medium feasibility (24-36 months, higher cost): Large-scale empirical compliance studies require multi-journal collaboration and funding. Accuracy studies of detection tools require computational resources and tool access. Low feasibility (3+ years, very high cost): Long-term longitudinal tracking requires sustained institutional support and may face publication bias if misconduct data are suppressed.
